title: Steve Bannon Convicted of Contempt of Congress for Defying Jan. 6 Subpoena
description_medium: A federal jury convicted Steve Bannon in July 2022 on two counts of contempt of Congress after he refused to appear for a deposition and produce documents requested by the House committee investigating the January 6 attack. Judge Carl Nichols sentenced him to four months in prison. Bannon remained free while appealing, and President Donald Trump pardoned him in January 2025.
description_long: On July 22, 2022, a federal jury found Steve Bannon guilty of two counts of contempt of Congress. One count concerned his refusal to appear for a deposition; the other concerned his refusal to produce documents in response to a subpoena from the House Select Committee investigating the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol. Bannon had argued that executive privilege excused his noncompliance, although he had left the White House in 2017. In October 2022, Judge Carl Nichols sentenced him to four months in prison and a $6,500 fine. Bannon remained free while his appeal proceeded. President Donald Trump later granted him a pardon in January 2025. The case concerned Bannon’s failure to comply with Congress’s subpoena; it was not a trial of his political views or of the Capitol attack itself. The supplied New York Times link covers Trump’s separate federal indictment and does not document these events, so the account relies on Justice Department releases specific to Bannon’s conviction and sentencing.

title: Trump Turns Georgia Booking Photo Into Campaign Fundraising Image
description_medium: After Donald Trump was booked at Fulton County Jail in Georgia on August 24, 2023, his campaign quickly used the resulting mugshot in fundraising appeals and merchandise. The image transformed a criminal booking into a political symbol for supporters. The campaign reported a sharp fundraising surge, but the amount in the supplied record is corrupted and is omitted here.
description_long: On August 24, 2023, Donald Trump surrendered at Fulton County Jail in Atlanta after being indicted in Georgia over efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election results. The booking produced a mugshot that his campaign quickly circulated and used in fundraising appeals and merchandise. The image recast the booking as a campaign symbol: Trump’s appeal presented the legal case as political persecution, while supporters could purchase items bearing the photograph. The campaign described a fundraising surge after the image’s release. An Associated Press report published days later quoted the campaign as saying it raised $7.1 million since the booking, including $4.18 million on Friday; those are campaign-reported figures, not independently audited totals. The packet’s own title and summary contain a corrupted amount, so this entry does not preserve that figure as fact. The linked New York Times article predates the booking and cannot establish its fundraising effect; the AP report provides same-event reporting.

title: House Republicans Launch Biden Impeachment Inquiry
description_medium: On September 12, 2023, Speaker Kevin McCarthy announced a formal House impeachment inquiry into President Joe Biden after months of Republican investigations into his family’s business dealings. McCarthy launched the inquiry without first holding a House vote, a choice that avoided testing support among Republicans. The White House called the move baseless; Republicans said the inquiry would gather evidence.
description_long: House Speaker Kevin McCarthy announced on September 12, 2023, that House Republicans would open an impeachment inquiry into President Joe Biden. The move followed months of investigations, led by Republican committees, into the business dealings of Biden’s son Hunter and whether the president had improperly benefited from them. McCarthy did not first hold a House vote authorizing the inquiry, avoiding a test of his narrow majority at a time when some Republicans were reluctant to support it. Republicans argued that the inquiry would give them a formal process to obtain documents and testimony. The White House rejected the effort as baseless and politically motivated. At the time of launch, the inquiry was an investigative step, not an impeachment vote or a finding that Biden had committed an offense. The supplied Reuters report described the announcement and the competing claims. A later House vote formally authorized the inquiry in December 2023, but the supplied material does not establish its complete later course or outcome.
source_access_notes: Supplied Reuters URL was not fetched successfully; search located Reuters syndicated reporting on the September 12 announcement and the lack of a prior House vote. Used the same-event Reuters report.
rationale: Adds the inquiry’s trigger, procedure, and opposing positions without stating allegations as proven. Keeps the launch distinct from formal authorization and impeachment.

title: Maine Secretary of State Removes Trump from Primary Ballot
description_medium: On December 28, 2023, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows ruled that Donald Trump was ineligible for the state’s Republican presidential primary ballot under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment. She concluded that his role in the January 6 attack disqualified him under the amendment’s insurrection clause. The decision was stayed during litigation and later proceedings awaited the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling.
description_long: Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows issued her decision on December 28, 2023, after voters challenged Donald Trump’s eligibility for the state’s Republican presidential primary. Bellows concluded that Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment barred him from the ballot because, after taking an oath to support the Constitution, he had engaged in insurrection related to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The decision made Maine the second state, after Colorado, to find Trump disqualified under Section 3, but it was the first such decision by a state election official acting on a challenge. Trump appealed. In January 2024, Maine’s highest court left the matter with the secretary of state and stayed the effect of her decision, by agreement of the parties, while the U.S. Supreme Court considered the related Colorado case. The Supreme Court later held that states could not enforce Section 3 against federal candidates. The linked New York Times story is about Trump’s January 6 speech, not Bellows’s ballot ruling; the description relies on Maine’s court record and contemporaneous AP reporting.

corrected_wording.text: The attached New York Times article covers Trump’s January 6 speech; it does not support the December 2023 Maine ballot ruling. Maine court records and AP reporting document the decision and stay.

source_access_notes: The supplied 2021 NYT link is unrelated. Used the Maine Supreme Judicial Court’s January 2024 decision and AP’s same-event report. The packet’s description that the stay awaited Supreme Court review is clarified as a litigation stay pending the Court’s related Colorado decision.
rationale: Explains the state decision, legal basis, appeal and stay while distinguishing a ballot ruling from a final national determination. Corrects the supplied source mismatch.
